$\,$ounces of peanuts." :question/worked-solution "We must write and evaluate an expression representing the total amount of peanuts.

Since each of them bought $6$ ounces of salted peanuts and $4$ ounces of unsalted peanuts, the amount of peanuts they purchased, in ounces, is:

$$
{{6}_{⏟}}_{\text{salted peanuts}}+{{4}_{⏟}}_{\text{unsalted peanuts}}
$$

Since *each* person purchased this amount of peanuts, and there are $2$ people, we must multiply the amount of peanuts by $2.$ Therefore, the total amount of peanuts is:

$$
{{(6+4)}_{⏟}}_{\text{each person}}\times {{2}_{⏟}}_{\text{people}}
$$

To evaluate the expression, we follow the order of operations with parentheses.

First, we perform the operations inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}(6+4)\times 2 & =(6+4)\times 2 \\  & =10\times 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply:

$$
10\times 2=20
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5349a1c7-9dd6-5f93-9b66-8b75dd18d825"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-5349a1c7-9dd6-5f93-9b66-8b75dd18d825" :answer-field/id #uuid "5349a1c7-9dd6-5f93-9b66-8b75dd18d825" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-48840b8b-45fc-5af4-9eaf-3b0433653b29" :answer-field/choices ["answer-48840b8b-45fc-5af4-9eaf-3b0433653b29"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-48840b8b-45fc-5af4-9eaf-3b0433653b29" :answer/id #uuid "48840b8b-45fc-5af4-9eaf-3b0433653b29" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "20" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059859 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b88dbf04-dd80-54e8-8fde-e4783f40c410"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-b88dbf04-dd80-54e8-8fde-e4783f40c410" :question/id #uuid "b88dbf04-dd80-54e8-8fde-e4783f40c410" :question/math-academy-id "q-134232" :question/problem "Carla has $12$ packages of almonds, each weighing $42$ ounces. $$

First, we multiply the ones:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} &  &  & \,\,\,\,\begin{aligned} \\ \boxed{0}\end{aligned}\,\,\,\, &  \\  &  &  & \,\,\,\,1\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,\times \,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, \\  &  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\,\end{aligned} & \,\, & \begin{aligned}12\times 2=24\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we multiply the tens:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} &  &  & \,\,\,\,\begin{aligned}\boxed{} \\ \boxed{0}\end{aligned}\,\,\,\, &  \\  &  &  & \,\,\,\,1\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,\times \,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, \\  &  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\, \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,8\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\,\end{aligned} & \,\, & \begin{aligned}12\times 40=480\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we add the results:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} &  &  & \,\,\,\,\begin{aligned}\boxed{} \\ \boxed{0}\end{aligned}\,\,\,\, &  \\  &  &  & \,\,\,\,1\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,\times \,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, \\  &  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,+\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,8\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\,\end{aligned} & \,\, & \begin{aligned}24+480=504\end{aligned} \\  & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $12\times 42=504.$

$\,$pounds of walnuts in total." :question/worked-solution "To determine the number of walnuts Robert and Susan bought together in total, we have to calculate the following sum:

$$
3+\frac{17}{9}
$$

To add $3$ and $\frac{17}{9},$ we need to express the whole number $3$ as an equivalent fraction with a denominator of $9.$

First, we write $3$ as an improper fraction:

$$
\frac{3}{1}
$$

Then we put this fraction over a denominator of $9$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $9:$

$$
\frac{3\times 9}{1\times 9}=\frac{27}{9}
$$

So now, we have to find:

$$
\frac{27}{9}+\frac{17}{9}
$$

To add two fractions with like denominators, we add the numerators and keep the denominators the same:

$$
\frac{27}{9}+\frac{17}{9}=\frac{27+17}{9}=\frac{44}{9}
$$

Expressing our answer as a mixed number, we have

$$
44÷9=4\,\text{R}\,8=4\,\frac{8}{9}.
$$

Therefore, they bought $4\,\frac{8}{9}$ pounds of walnuts." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-61d4181d-edef-5c2f-bb3f-ce5a078247b4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-61d4181d-edef-5c2f-bb3f-ce5a078247b4" :answer-field/id #uuid "61d4181d-edef-5c2f-bb3f-ce5a078247b4" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-186dfbec-40e1-5669-b78b-1a6e666b138c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-186dfbec-40e1-5669-b78b-1a6e666b138c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-186dfbec-40e1-5669-b78b-1a6e666b138c" :answer/id #uuid "186dfbec-40e1-5669-b78b-1a6e666b138c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\frac{8}{9}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186073826 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-357eb628-a446-5e21-9526-dabfe7335132"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-357eb628-a446-5e21-9526-dabfe7335132" :question/id #uuid "357eb628-a446-5e21-9526-dabfe7335132" :question/math-academy-id "q-134235" :question/problem "Of the $3$ pounds of walnuts that Robert bought, he gave $\frac{3}{5}$ pounds to his granddaughter Sophia. pounds of walnuts remaining." :question/worked-solution "To find out how many walnuts Robert had remaining, we must calculate the difference $3-\frac{3}{5}.$

To subtract $\frac{3}{5}$ from $3,$ we need to express the whole number $3$ as an equivalent fraction with a denominator of $5.$

First, we write $3$ as an improper fraction:

$$
\frac{3}{1}
$$

Then, we put this fraction over a denominator of $5$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $5:$

$$
\frac{3\times 5}{1\times 5}=\frac{15}{5}
$$

So now, we have to find:

$$
\frac{15}{5}-\frac{3}{5}
$$

To subtract two fractions with like denominators, we subtract the numerators and keep the denominators the same. Therefore:

$$
\frac{15}{5}-\frac{3}{5}=\frac{15-3}{5}=\frac{12}{5}
$$

Finally, we convert to a mixed number:

$$
12÷5=2\,\text{R}\,2=2\,\frac{2}{5}
$$

Therefore, Robert had $2\,\frac{2}{5}$ pounds of walnuts remaining." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-34368c67-3db4-5d2a-b4a5-7e644a1384c1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-34368c67-3db4-5d2a-b4a5-7e644a1384c1" :answer-field/id #uuid "34368c67-3db4-5d2a-b4a5-7e644a1384c1" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-f7eeccef-0153-5dbc-86a4-c355fb99fe59" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f7eeccef-0153-5dbc-86a4-c355fb99fe59"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f7eeccef-0153-5dbc-86a4-c355fb99fe59" :answer/id #uuid "f7eeccef-0153-5dbc-86a4-c355fb99fe59" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\frac{2}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198431 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-994437db-5e6c-52cd-85e4-193a53ab9c7f"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-994437db-5e6c-52cd-85e4-193a53ab9c7f" :question/id #uuid "994437db-5e6c-52cd-85e4-193a53ab9c7f" :question/math-academy-id "q-134236" :question/problem "After Sophia takes her share of walnuts, Robert's remaining amount of walnuts is{{field-1}}

{{field-2}} $\frac{17}{9}.$" :question/worked-solution "Robert has $2\,\frac{2}{5}$ pounds of walnuts remaining, and Susan has $\frac{17}{9}$ pounds of walnuts.

We cannot compare the fractions directly as they don't have a common denominator.

We can make a common denominator of $5\times 9=45.$

To put $2\,\frac{2}{5}$ over a denominator of $45,$ we first convert to an improper fraction and then multiply the numerator and denominator by $9:$

$$
2\,\frac{2}{5}=\frac{12}{5}=\frac{12\times 9}{5\times 9}=\frac{108}{45}
$$

To put $\frac{17}{9}$ over a denominator of $45,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator by $5:$

$$
\frac{17}{9}=\frac{17\times 5}{9\times 5}=\frac{85}{45}
$$

We can now compare the fractions $\frac{108}{45}$ and $\frac{85}{45}$ by looking at the numerators only.

Since $108>85,$ the correct statement must be:

$$
\frac{108}{45}>\frac{85}{45}
$$

So, the correct answer is

> "After Sophia takes her walnuts, Robert's remaining amount of walnuts is $>$ than Susan's amount of walnuts because $2\,\frac{2}{5}>\frac{17}{9}.$"" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8fcd58ca-53e4-51a1-8c9a-e0b485e4a754" "answer-field-89dc9221-5a2e-543b-a0cb-442c6540822e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8fcd58ca-53e4-51a1-8c9a-e0b485e4a754" :answer-field/id #uuid "8fcd58ca-53e4-51a1-8c9a-e0b485e4a754" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-4d48c43c-8024-5436-8502-563ff420ec3c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4d48c43c-8024-5436-8502-563ff420ec3c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4d48c43c-8024-5436-8502-563ff420ec3c" :answer/id #uuid "4d48c43c-8024-5436-8502-563ff420ec3c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value ">" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-89dc9221-5a2e-543b-a0cb-442c6540822e" :answer-field/id #uuid "89dc9221-5a2e-543b-a0cb-442c6540822e" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-f46a10ec-6f4d-59dd-a288-fa100b9f0e3d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f46a10ec-6f4d-59dd-a288-fa100b9f0e3d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f46a10ec-6f4d-59dd-a288-fa100b9f0e3d" :answer/id #uuid "f46a10ec-6f4d-59dd-a288-fa100b9f0e3d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value ">" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186142796 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-56c0d0ac-e441-53cb-9b72-c25279d28ac0"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-56c0d0ac-e441-53cb-9b72-c25279d28ac0" :question/id #uuid "56c0d0ac-e441-53cb-9b72-c25279d28ac0" :question/math-academy-id "q-134237" :question/problem "Susan ate $\frac{1}{3}$ of the walnuts that she bought. $$

$$

$$

We can now compare the fractions $\frac{108}{45}$ and $\frac{85}{45}$ by looking at the numerators only.

Since $108>85,$ the correct statement must be:

$$
\frac{108}{45}>\frac{85}{45}
$$

brackets, the order of operations with parentheses tells us to:\n\n- Calculate the operations in the parentheses *first*.\n- Calculate the operations in square brackets *second*.\n- Finally, follow the order of operations, as usual.\n\nTo illustrate, let's evaluate the following expression:\n\n$$\n1+ [2 \\times (3 + 4)]\n$$\n\nFirst, we perform the operation inside the :step/content {:db/id 17592186060868 :tutorial/content "We can use the standard algorithm to multiply two-digit numbers.\n\nTo illustrate, let's use the standard algorithm to compute $12\\times 13$.\n\nRecall that ${\\color{blue}1}{\\color{red}3}$ in expanded form is ${\\color{blue}10} + {\\color{red}3}$. The idea is to first multiply $12$ by ${\\color{red}3}$, then by ${\\color{blue}10}$, and add the results.\n\nWe write one number above the other as follows:\n\n$$\n1\\begin{vmatrix}2 \\\\ \\cdot\\end{vmatrix}0\\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 & 3\\end{vmatrix}36 + 120 = 156\n$$\n\nFirst, we multiply the top number ($12$) by the value in the ones place of the second number ($\\bbox[2px, lightgray]{3}$), writing the result under the line:\n\n$$\n1\\begin{vmatrix}2 \\\\ \\cdot\\end{vmatrix}0\\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1\\end{vmatrix}3; 3 \\mid 6 \\mid 12 \\cdot 3 = 36000\n$$\n\nNext, we multiply $12$ by $\\bbox[2px, lightgray]{1}0$. Let's do this in steps:\n\n**Step 1**: Any number multiplied by $10$ always gives a zero at the end. Therefore, we place a zero in the ones column underneath our first result.\n\n$$\n1\\begin{vmatrix}2 \\\\ \\cdot\\end{vmatrix}0\\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1\\end{vmatrix}3; 3\\begin{vmatrix}6 \\\\ 0\\end{vmatrix}12 \\cdot 10 = 1200\n$$\n\n**Step 2**: Now, we work out $\\bbox[2px, lightgray]{2}\\times \\bbox[2px, lightgray]{1}$. We place the answer next to our zero:\n\n$$\n1\\begin{vmatrix}2 \\\\ \\cdot\\end{vmatrix}0\\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1\\end{vmatrix}3; 3\\begin{vmatrix}6 \\\\ 2\\end{vmatrix}0 \\mid 2 \\cdot 1 = 20\n$$\n\n**Step 3**: Next, we we work out $\\bbox[2px, lightgray]{1}\\times \\bbox[2px, lightgray]{1}$:\n\n$$\n1\\begin{vmatrix}2 \\\\ \\cdot\\end{vmatrix}0\\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1\\end{vmatrix}3; 3\\begin{vmatrix}6 \\\\ 1\\end{vmatrix}2 \\mid 0 \\mid 1 \\cdot 1 = 10\n$$\n\nFinally, we add the results:\n\n$$\n1\\begin{vmatrix}2 \\\\ \\cdot\\end{vmatrix}0\\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1\\end{vmatrix}3; 3\\begin{vmatrix}6 \\\\ +\\end{vmatrix}1\\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\\\ 1 & 5\\end{vmatrix}6 \\mid 36 + 120 = 156\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n12 \\times 13 = 156\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c5e81bce-1ac7-5040-8119-b2548f14f16f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1758 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c65146f8-f7f2-5175-8f4b-ccbf6a287fdc" :step/math-academy-id 5324 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060829}} {:db/id 17592186060829 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059857 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059455 :question/id #uuid "fe28e925-3711-5bd4-8937-22072ba23ddf" :question/math-academy-id "e-1646"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "06797272-eabc-558c-8528-aae8b6166c02" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049410} {:db/id 17592186050248} {:db/id 17592186050735}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060307} {:db/id 17592186060308}] :knowledge-point/title "Multiplying a Two-Digit Number by a Two-Digit Number"} :step/id #uuid "469e26a7-ca8d-5fb8-91ed-400f5368f8de" :step/math-academy-id 5325 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060830}} {:db/id 17592186060830 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060869 :tutorial/content "Just like when multiplying a number by a one-digit number, we will sometimes have carries. Let's do this in steps.\n\n**Step 1**: We start by writing a zero:\n\n$$\n0; [math]\\color{blue}\\phantom{0}[/math]; 2\\begin{vmatrix}4 \\\\ \\cdot\\end{vmatrix}0\\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3\\end{vmatrix}2; {\\color{blue}1}{\\color{red}2}\n$$\n\nWe carry the ${\\color{blue}1}$ and write down $\\color{red}2$:\n\n$$\n[math]\\color{blue}1[/math]; [math]\\color{blue}\\phantom{0}[/math]; 2\\begin{vmatrix}4 \\\\ \\cdot\\end{vmatrix}0\\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3\\end{vmatrix}2; 4\\begin{vmatrix}8 \\\\ 2\\end{vmatrix}0 \\mid 4 \\cdot 3 = 12; Carry:1; Write:2\n$$\n\n**Step 3**: We multiply\n\n$$\n\\bbox[2px, lightgray]{2}\\times \\bbox[2px, lightgray]{3} = 6\n$$\n\nand we add the carry from the previous multiplication to make\n\n$$\n6+{\\color{blue}{1}} = {\\color{red}{7}}\n$$\n\n$$\n[math]\\color{blue}1[/math]; [math]\\color{blue}\\phantom{0}[/math]; 2\\begin{vmatrix}4 \\\\ \\cdot\\end{vmatrix}0\\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3\\end{vmatrix}2; 4\\begin{vmatrix}8 \\\\ 7\\end{vmatrix}2 \\mid 0 \\mid 2 \\cdot 3 = 6and6 + 1 = 7; Carry: -; Write:7\n$$\n\nFinally, we add the results:\n\n$$\n[math]\\color{blue}1[/math]; [math]\\color{blue}\\phantom{0}[/math]; :step/math-academy-id 45216} {:db/id 17592186199367 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199497 :tutorial/content "We saw how to compare fraction models using common denominators in a previous lesson. In this lesson, we'll learn how to carry out these processes without models.\n\nFor example, suppose we have the following two fractions:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{1}{\\color{blue}3} \\qquad \\dfrac{4}{\\color{red}6}\n$$\n\nWhich of them is larger?\n\nAt the moment, it's difficult to compare them as they don't have a common denominator. Therefore, we must *create* a common denominator.\n\nNotice that our denominators are ${\\color{blue}3}$ and ${\\color{red}{6}}$, and ${\\color{red}{6}}$ is a multiple of ${\\color{blue}3}$. In fact,\n\n$$\n{\\color{red}{6}} = {\\color{purple}{2}} \\times {\\color{blue}3}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we can create a common denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of the *first* fraction by ${\\color{purple}{2}}$, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\frac{1}{3} &= \\frac{1 \\cdot 2}{3 \\cdot 2} = \\frac{2}{6}\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we now have the following two fractions:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{2}{\\color{red}6} \\qquad \\dfrac{4}{\\color{red}6}\n$$\n\nFrom here, it's easy to see that the second fraction is larger. So, we have\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{2}{\\color{red}6} < \\dfrac{4}{\\color{red}6}\\,\n$$\n\nTherefore, we conclude that\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{1}{\\color{blue}3} < \\dfrac{4}{\\color{red}6}\n$$\n\nLet's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "f0d25e8e-bb9e-50d9-b3d0-fd69a9943adb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7821 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b29119b6-dd48-5ca3-b83d-aa49d38cb72e" :step/math-academy-id 45243 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199364}} {:db/id 17592186199385 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199511 :tutorial/content "Consider the following fractions:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{1}{\\color{blue}2} \\qquad \\dfrac{1}{\\color{red}3}\n$$\n\nLet's compare these fractions using common denominators.\n\nNotice that ${\\color{red}3}$ is *not* a multiple of ${\\color{blue}2}$. However, we can create a common denominator by taking the product of the denominators.\n\nIn this case, our common denominator will be\n\n$$\n{\\color{blue}2} \\times {\\color{red}3} = 6\n$$\n\n- To put $\\dfrac12$ over a denominator of $6$, we multiply the numerator and denominator by ${\\color{red}3}{:}$\n$\\frac{1}{2} = \\frac{1 \\cdot 3}{2 \\cdot 3} = \\frac{3}{6}$\n- To put $\\dfrac13$ over a denominator of $6$, we multiply the numerator and denominator by ${\\color{blue}2}{:}$\n$\\frac{1}{3} = \\frac{1 \\cdot 2}{3 \\cdot 2} = \\frac{2}{6}$\n\nSo, we now have the following two fractions:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac36 \\qquad\\dfrac26\n$$\n\nFrom here, it's easy to see that the first fraction is larger. So, we have\n\n$$\n\\dfrac36 > \\dfrac26\n$$\n\nTherefore, we conclude that\n\n$$\n\\dfrac12 > \\dfrac13\n$$\n\nLet's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "6d0d99a2-4c43-5268-82e8-cb9f2c133f94" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7921 :tutorial/title "Cases Where the Least Common Denominator Is a Product of the Denominators"} :step/id #uuid "ff41765d-5768-5be7-b7c9-fc631dd1a47b" :step/math-academy-id 45627 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199365}} {:db/id 17592186199386 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199512 :tutorial/content "Whenever two denominators have a common factor greater than $1$, the most efficient way to find a least common denominator is to look at the denominators' multiples.\n\nFor example, consider the following fractions:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{2}{\\color{blue}6} \\qquad \\dfrac{5}{\\color{red}9}\n$$\n\nNotice that ${\\color{blue}6}$ and ${\\color{red}9}$ have $3$ as a common factor. This suggests that we can create a common denominator by looking at their least common multiples:\n\n- Multiples of $6{:}\\qquad 6,12,{\\color{purple}{18}},24,\\ldots$\n- Multiples of $9{:}\\qquad 9,{\\color{purple}{18}},27,36,\\ldots$\n\nTherefore, our least common denominator will be ${\\color{purple}{18}}$.\n\n- To put $\\dfrac26$ over a denominator of $18$, we multiply the numerator and denominator by $3{:}$\n$\\frac{2}{6} = \\frac{2 \\cdot 3}{6 \\cdot 3} = \\frac{6}{18}$\n- To put $\\dfrac59$ over a denominator of $18$, we multiply the numerator and denominator by $2{:}$\n$\\frac{5}{9} = \\frac{5 \\cdot 2}{9 \\cdot 2} = \\frac{10}{18}$\n\nSo, we now have the following two fractions:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{6}{18} \\qquad\\dfrac{10}{18}\n$$\n\nFrom here, it's easy to see that the second fraction is larger. So, we have\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{2}{\\color{red}6} < \\dfrac{4}{\\color{red}6}\\,\n$$\n\nTherefore, we conclude that\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{1}{\\color{blue}3} < \\dfrac{4}{\\color{red}6}\n$$\n\nLet's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "f0d25e8e-bb9e-50d9-b3d0-fd69a9943adb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7821 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186199511 :tutorial/content "Consider the following fractions:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{1}{\\color{blue}2} \\qquad \\dfrac{1}{\\color{red}3}\n$$\n\nLet's compare these fractions using common denominators.\n\nNotice that ${\\color{red}3}$ is *not* a multiple of ${\\color{blue}2}$. So, we have\n\n$$\n\\dfrac36 > \\dfrac26\n$$\n\nTherefore, we conclude that\n\n$$\n\\dfrac12 > \\dfrac13\n$$\n\nLet's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "6d0d99a2-4c43-5268-82e8-cb9f2c133f94" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7921 :tutorial/title "Cases Where the Least Common Denominator Is a Product of the Denominators"} {:db/id 17592186199512 :tutorial/content "Whenever two denominators have a common factor greater than $1$, the most efficient way to find a least common denominator is to look at the denominators' multiples.\n\nFor example, consider the following fractions:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{2}{\\color{blue}6} \\qquad \\dfrac{5}{\\color{red}9}\n$$\n\nNotice that ${\\color{blue}6}$ and ${\\color{red}9}$ have $3$ as a common factor.
